item.title: Synaptic Dendritic Neuron Model (scDNM) for Cell Type Classification in Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.10207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cell type classification in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is challenging because of high dimensionality, sparsity, and transcriptionally similar cell types. We developed scDNM, an adaptation of the dendritic neuron model incorporating learnable synaptic thresholds, a supervised gene pool, staged training, and ensemble prediction. Six binary classification tasks were constructed from the Paul15, PBMC3k, and Nestorowa datasets. All models were evaluated using leakage-free nested cross-validation, with feature selection, scaling, and hyperparameter tuning performed independently of the outer test folds. scDNM ranked first in three of six tasks (including one tie) and achieved the best mean accuracy rank (2.00), followed by XGBoost (2.75), Random Forest (3.33), logistic regression (3.33), and SVM (3.58). In a six-class PBMC3k experiment, scDNM achieved 95.997% accuracy and 0.944 macro-F1, compared with 94.243% and 0.914 for SingleR. Garnett returned only Unknown labels and was treated as a zero-coverage technical outcome. Ablation analysis supported the contributions of dendrites and synaptic thresholds. However, XGBoost achieved higher mean binary-task accuracy (96.20% versus 95.32% for scDNM), and across-task rank differences were not statistically significant. These findings demonstrate that scDNM is competitive for scRNA-seq cell type classification, although broader independent validation is required.
item.dc:creator: Deniz Karap{\i}nar, Gaurav Choudhary, Melih Agraz

item.title: Publications as benchmarks: auditing AI agents on spatial transcriptomics alignment
item.description: arXiv:2611.11796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents are increasingly automating data analysis, but responsible adoption requires reliable performance evaluation, which is costly in specialized scientific domains. We introduce a framework that translates scientific publications into auditable benchmarks for AI agents and demonstrate its use on spatial transcriptomics alignment tasks. Across 121 tasks, 16 baseline methods, and six AI agents, the best agents (GPT-6-Astra and Gemini-4-Argon) matched or outperformed all baselines on 80% of tasks, often using surprisingly simple heuristics. Agent performance was robust to prompting and access to pre-installed packages. Benchmark construction also uncovered errors in prior work and shortcuts in current evaluation metrics. Finally, we show that agent-generated solutions can be distilled into a reusable program that ranks in the top 10% of baseline methods on unseen data. Our framework offers a scalable way to evaluate AI agents in specialized scientific domains by leveraging and stress-testing existing papers and metrics.
item.dc:creator: Yiqun T. Chen, Jan Matthias, Jianing Yao, Hongyu Eric Zhao, Stephanie C. Hicks

item.title: Pruning DNA Sequence
item.description: arXiv:2611.10386v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Data pruning can substantially reduce training cost by removing examples that contribute little additional learning signal, but it has not been studied for DNA language-model pretraining. We introduce Sequence Pruning (SP), a dynamic pruning framework that removes genomic sequences as they become easy for the model to predict. SP uses per-sequence pretraining accuracy computed directly from the model's forward pass, requiring no separate scoring model or additional pass over the corpus. We evaluate SP across five pretraining settings spanning two corpora, three model families, and both MLM and CLM objectives, with downstream evaluation on five genomic benchmarks. SP reduces pretraining data processing by up to 96% while largely preserving downstream performance. At moderate savings, pruning improves performance by up to 1.2 MCC points over full-data pretraining; at the highest savings, pretraining uses only 4% of the baseline GPU hours with little performance loss. SP also outperforms the dynamic pruning methods InfoBatch and BPAS across most comparisons. Beyond accuracy, our framework supports alternative criteria such as perplexity and EL2N, although accuracy yields the strongest downstream performance at matched savings. These results show that genomic pretraining does not require repeatedly processing all available sequences and that dynamic sequence-level pruning can substantially improve its data and computational efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/FaiasPromit/pruning-dna-sequence.
item.dc:creator: Faias Satter, Shaker Islam, Aminul Islam

item.title: When gene summaries reveal the answers: Gene Ontology circularity in gene embedding benchmarks
item.description: arXiv:2611.11118v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A gene summary can contain the very annotations used to evaluate an embedding of its text. The Alliance of Genome Resources converts Gene Ontology (GO) annotations into sentences, which NCBI Gene displays and GenePT includes in its input. These summaries covered 6,172 of 19,256 human protein-coding genes (32.1%), including 58% of genes with one to ten linked publications. We embedded the same corpus with and without the generated summaries and refitted a function-prediction probe on each version. Among genes with one to ten publications, removal reduced the reported per-gene area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) by 0.078 with a linear probe (95% bootstrap interval 0.072-0.084) and by 0.033 with a multilayer perceptron. These estimates use a historical GO scorer that mishandled ties. The original predictions are unavailable for rescoring. A simple TF-IDF encoder also benefited from the summaries, as did models evaluated only on experimental annotations. Replacing generated summaries with UniProt function descriptions recovered much of the lost performance despite little verbatim overlap. UniProt also curates many of the evaluation labels. In mouse and yeast, we found a similar dependence on the source of the description. We introduce GeneProv to compare encoders on matched text and to examine how representation rankings change across GO recovery, non-GO endpoints and co-essentiality.
item.dc:creator: Jiawei Wu, Huishu Wang, Junlin Chen, Hongyi Wang

item.title: scBIG++: Learning Across Genes and Cells to Predict Single-Cell Perturbation Responses
item.description: arXiv:2611.11217v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Predicting single-cell transcriptional responses to genetic and chemical interventions supports gene-function discovery and regulatory analysis. Existing studies often focus only on highly variable genes, restricting the expression changes available for downstream analysis. Cells exposed to the same intervention can also show heterogeneous expression responses, with coordinated gene programs active to different degrees. We propose scBIG++, a full-gene perturbation prediction framework that models this heterogeneity by connecting expression-adaptive gene modules with population-conditioned generation. To preserve shared gene structure while accommodating cellular variation, Gene-Relation Clustering organizes genes into common windows, within which Dynamic SoftSub learns expression-dependent submodule memberships. This shared organization enables Set-GCAE to exchange information about corresponding gene groups across control cells, placing individual representations in their source-population context. The cell representations initialize a latent flow, while their pooled summary and the perturbation representation condition response generation. Generated states are decoded into expression profiles covering all assayed protein-coding genes retained after preprocessing, supporting comprehensive analysis of perturbation-induced expression changes. Experiments across six genetic and chemical settings spanning 6,539--19,451 genes demonstrate competitive perturbation-effect recovery and full-gene expression reconstruction under unseen targets and combinations, cross-cell-line transfer, and held-out compounds. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ttruan2426-dot/scBIG.
item.dc:creator: Jiafa Ruan, Zican Qiao, Zongxin Yang, Ruijie Quan, Yi Yang

item.title: Reproducible quantum clustering for single-cell transcriptome atlases
item.description: arXiv:2611.11745v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Current single-cell clustering pipelines discard most genes and can yield inconsistent clusters across random seeds. We introduce KQE-2, a training-free hybrid quantum-classical framework for reproducible whole-transcriptome clustering. KQE-2 maps cells into entanglement-free quantum states, enabling exact feature evaluation on classical hardware and direct checks on a quantum processor. Theoretically, we prove that removing entanglement is necessary and sufficient to bound single-qubit feature variance locally. Practically, while retraining scVI shifted 14% of cells and altered rare-type markers and drug targets, KQE-2 delivered identical biology across runs. On standard highly variable genes, the quantum encoding alone raised accuracy on a developing cortex from 0.61 to 0.79. KQE-2 scales to 11.4 million nuclei on one server, outperforming the compared methods on eight of ten complete atlases (and within the best method's run-to-run range on two), and leads on six even under standard downstream clustering.
item.dc:creator: Henry Han

item.title: Robust Machine Learning for Regulatory Sequence Modeling under Biological and Technical Distribution Shifts
item.description: arXiv:2601.14969v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robust machine learning for regulatory genomics is studied under biologically and technically induced distribution shifts. Deep convolutional and attention-based models achieve strong in-distribution performance on DNA regulatory sequence prediction tasks but are usually evaluated under i.i.d. assumptions, even though real applications involve cell type-specific programs, evolutionary turnover, assay protocol changes, and sequencing artifacts. We introduce a robustness framework that combines a mechanistic simulation benchmark with real data analysis on an MPRA dataset to quantify performance degradation, calibration failures, and uncertainty-based reliability. In simulation, motif-driven regulatory outputs are generated with cell type-specific programs, PWM perturbations, GC bias, depth variation, batch effects, and heteroscedastic noise, and CNN, BiLSTM, and transformer models are evaluated. Models remain accurate and reasonably calibrated under mild GC content shifts but show higher error, severe variance miscalibration, and coverage collapse under motif effect rewiring and noise-dominated regimes, revealing robustness gaps invisible to standard i.i.d. evaluation. Adding simple biological structural priors, motif-derived features in simulation, and global GC content in MPRA improves distribution error and yields consistent robustness gains under biologically meaningful genomic shifts, while providing only limited protection against strong assay noise. Uncertainty-aware selective prediction offers an additional safety layer, and risk coverage analyses on simulated and MPRA data show that filtering low-confidence inputs recovers low-risk subsets, including under GC-based OOD conditions, although reliability gains diminish when noise dominates.
item.dc:creator: Yiyao Yang

item.title: Simple models outperform single-cell foundation models on downstream benchmarks
item.description: arXiv:2602.16696v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data exhibit strong and reproducible statistical structure. This has motivated the development of large-scale foundation models, such as TranscriptFormer, that use transformer-based architectures to learn a generative model for gene expression by embedding genes into a latent vector space. These embeddings have been used to obtain state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on downstream tasks such as cell-type classification, disease-state prediction, and cross-species learning. Here, we ask whether similar performance can be achieved without utilizing computationally intensive deep learning-based representations. Using simple, interpretable pipelines that rely on careful normalization and linear methods, we obtain SOTA or near SOTA performance across multiple benchmarks commonly used to evaluate single-cell foundation models, including outperforming foundation models on out-of-distribution tasks involving novel cell types and organisms absent from the training data. Our findings highlight the need for rigorous benchmarking and suggest that the biology of cell identity can be captured by simple linear representations of single cell gene expression data.
item.dc:creator: Huan Souza, Pankaj Mehta

item.title: GeneZip: Region-Aware Compression for Long Context DNA Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2602.17739v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-context DNA modeling is computationally expensive, motivating existing approaches to reduce sequence length through uniform downsampling. However, functional information and sequence redundancy are unevenly distributed across the genome, calling for finer resolution in functionally dense regions and stronger compression of redundant sequence. We introduce GeneZip, a region-aware DNA compression framework that learns where to allocate a limited token budget. Building on H-Net-style dynamic routing, GeneZip combines a Region-Aware Ratio objective, which uses regional labels derived from GENCODE gene annotations to specify compression targets during training, with bounded routing for stable token counts. At inference, it compresses raw DNA without annotations. GeneZip provides three main benefits. First, it preserves predictive utility under high compression: GeneZip-70M achieves 137.6-fold compression with a validation perplexity increase of 0.31 relative to uncompressed Mamba2-84M, and the best average rank across four DNALongBench tasks among compression models with leakage-controlled pretraining. Second, it learns region-aware allocation with emergent repeat-aware compression. Alternative regional priors yield task-dependent performance trade-offs. Without repeat-specific supervision, GeneZip compresses transposable-element-derived and tandem repeats more strongly than matched non-repeat sequence; its tandem-repeat compression preference transfers to a nine-species evaluation panel without further training. Third, it enables efficient long-context modeling: on 450-kb inputs, GeneZip-70M achieves 36.1-fold higher inference throughput than JanusDNA-7.7M on a single H100 GPU.
item.dc:creator: Jianan Zhao, Xixian Liu, Zhihao Zhan, Xinyu Yuan, Hongyu Guo, Jian Tang

item.title: PEN-STACK: A provenance-enforcing tool layer for language-model agents in genome writing
item.description: arXiv:2608.20412v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Writing a gene into a human genome is a coupled design problem across locus, writer enzyme, cargo and delivery vehicle. Language-model agents are widely applied to such problems, but genome writing has no grounded tool layer. We present PEN-STACK, an open tool layer with enforced provenance that exposes ten design stages as twenty-two scope-aware tools over SDK, Model Context Protocol and REST interfaces. It integrates chromatin, enzyme, off-target, delivery and immunogenicity evidence under one typed contract: every reported quantity originates from a validated tool, and anything out of scope returns an explicit known-unknown. Given no tools and a naive prompt, three model families fabricated 97.1% to 100.0% of 240 required quantities. Coaching against fabrication reduced this to 0 of 240 on each of two families and 5 of 240 on a 1.5B-parameter local model, but each measured zero carries a 95% upper bound of 1.58%, so prompting yields no model-independent guarantee. With tool access on the same forty goals, all three families fabricated nothing, but 81% and 84% of required quantities resolved through a tool call for the two larger models against 27% for the local model: grounding confers fabrication safety, not capability. A pre-emission biosecurity screen matched its own probe specification on all eight designs, a self-consistency check with unmeasured error rates. A human position-effect model validated on held-out chromosomes (Spearman rho = 0.571, n = 1,506) but not on the features served by default (rho ~ 0.16), where the service withholds its validation flag. Ten claims were pre-specified in hash-locked specifications, though priority over scoring is not independently established; every outcome, including eight non-passes, is a machine-readable flag. Insertional-oncogenesis coverage is limited to documented loci. Code and three data resources are released openly.
item.dc:creator: Anees Ahmed Mahaboob Ali, Radhakrishnan Delhibabu, Everette Jacob Remington Nelson

item.title: BioFirewall: A genome-writing-native governance layer for design-stage biosecurity screening of agentic AI
item.description: arXiv:2608.20413v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI design tools now plan genome-scale edits, and agentic systems execute those plans with progressively less human oversight. Biosecurity controls are limited to two points: refusal guardrails at the foundation model and sequence-identity screening at the synthesiser. The design stage between them, where the plan is specified, is governed by recommendations, not by any deployed system. We present BioFirewall, a rule-governed middleware that intercepts a genome-writing plan and returns allow, flag-for-review, or refuse across five genome-writing-native hazard axes: cargo, locus, edit type, germline and scale, with cited evidence, a signed design passport, a tamper-evident audit log, and tiered access. On a de-circularised benchmark of safe proxies scored against independent oracles, a function-aware cargo classifier reached a true-positive rate of 0.72 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.89) at a false-positive rate of 1.105%, the nearest attainable to 1%, on a held-out split. Language-model judges did not reliably screen these sequences: their engagement depended heavily on sequence class, so a rate conditioned on engagement does not measure screening performance. Under prompt injection, the blocking verdicts of the open-weight judges tested flipped to allow, while the deterministic screen remained invariant. None of the 288 legitimate plans was refused, giving a 95% upper bound on the false-refuse rate of 0.0103 for the evaluated corpus under an independence assumption, or 0.632 treating the three plan templates as independent units. On a held-out gene set, the locus axis was enriched for drivers of in vivo insertional oncogenesis (AUROC 0.605; odds ratio 3.34), and a session monitor intercepted the cross-call decomposition attacks it was built to detect. These results show design-stage governance is achievable within the evaluated scope. BioFirewall is open source under a permissive licence.
item.dc:creator: Anees Ahmed Mahaboob Ali, Radhakrishnan Delhibabu, Everette Jacob Remington Nelson

item.title: Rethinking One Gene, One Token: Transcriptome-Aware Tokenization for Single-Cell Foundation Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.05410v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Single-cell foundation models typically treat each gene as a token, which is both costly and wasteful. A cell can express thousands of genes, so one token per gene makes self-attention expensive, yet many of these genes are detected at low levels and carry too little signal to deserve a token of their own. Genes that are expressed together could instead share a token, leaving separate tokens for genes that stand out. We introduce scTAT (Transcriptome-Aware Tokenization), which pairs a gene-set vocabulary with a per-cell tokenizer. The vocabulary holds overlapping gene sets that recur with stable relative expression across the pretraining corpus. Using these sets raises two difficulties. First, which genes should share a token depends on the cell, whereas existing multi-gene tokens fix the grouping in advance. Second, gene sets of different sizes must be compared with single genes on a common scale. The tokenizer therefore decides per cell, letting gene sets and single genes compete for token positions under an expression score normalized by the square root of set size. Training still reconstructs individual genes, so predictions stay at gene resolution. In frozen-embedding cell-type annotation, scTAT matches the strongest one-gene-per-token model with half the token budget. Its advantage over one-gene-per-token models at the same budget grows as the budget shrinks and the tokenizer assigns more positions to gene sets. Encoding the same genes with gene-set tokens also nearly halves the Transformer's matrix-multiplication cost. These results show that a token need not hold exactly one gene: when the tokenizer decides per cell which genes share a token, a fixed budget covers more of each transcriptome at no cost in annotation accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Jiaqi Xiong, Jiaying Li, Yu Zheng, Xiang Zhou, Ziteng Wang, Xinting Hu, Jiaxin Qi

item.title: Chem-PerturBridge: a harmonized compendium of small molecule perturbation transcriptomic effects
item.description: arXiv:2605.31522v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large perturbation models require training data encompassing chemical, cellular, and assay diversity. Current transcriptomic resources for small-molecule modeling, however, are fragmented across technologies, metadata conventions, controls, doses, and preprocessing pipelines. We introduce Chem-PerturBridge, a harmonized multi-dataset resource comprising over 37k compounds, 136 cellular contexts, and 1.25M transcriptomic samples across eight assay types, with standardized identifiers, metadata, and replicate-aware condition-level effects. We use the resource to evaluate matched-condition agreement across datasets and replicate agreement within datasets. Matched same-compound conditions show weak absolute agreement in fine-grained $\mathrm{logFC}$ rankings and magnitudes across most dataset pairs. However, they generally exceed individual same-context different-compound signatures, while often falling below the smoothed centroid of such signatures. Same-compound retrieval is above chance in all pairs. $\mathrm{LogFC}$ direction agreement is high in absolute terms, and exceeds both baselines in most cases. We further evaluate Chem-PerturBridge as a pretraining resource for compound representation learning. Under a compound-held-out OP3 evaluation split, embeddings pretrained on Chem-PerturBridge improve over L1000-only embeddings, Morgan fingerprints, chemical language model embeddings, and the descriptor-free OP3 baseline across metrics. An extensive molecule-holdout evaluation across 11 datasets further shows that models trained on Chem-PerturBridge outperform or match those that are not. Chem-PerturBridge therefore supports both diagnostic evaluation of cross-dataset signature agreement and model-oriented reuse of heterogeneous perturbation transcriptomic data.
item.dc:creator: Artur Sza{\l}ata, Olga Novitskaia, Maiia Shulman, Matthew Mella, Altynbek Zhubanchaliyev, Fabian J. Theis

item.title: Taxonomic Classification with Tag Arrays
item.description: arXiv:2610.10500v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a tool, KATKA, for taxonomic classification with tag arrays. Compared to Ahmed et al.'s state-of-the-art tool Cliffy ({\it Genome Research}, 2025) on the SILVA dataset from their paper and a readset similar to one of theirs, KATKA is faster, more accurate, much smaller and drastically easier to build.
item.dc:creator: Travis Gagie, Gonzalo Navarro
